propositions.text: PRRA officer unreasonably found no well-founded fear of persecution based on mental illness and gender.
propositions.quote: She argues that the PRRA officer unreasonably found that she would not have a well-founded fear of persecution based on mental illness and gender upon returning to her country of origin, Djibouti.

propositions.text: Dismissing application because officer's analysis was reasonable and based on established legal principles.
propositions.quote: I am dismissing her application, because the officer’s analysis of the evidence was reasonable and based on established legal principles.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues PRRA officer unreasonably found no persecution fear; court dismisses application as officer's analysis was reasonable.

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar is a Djibouti citizen who fled to Canada after alleged police assault and store closure due to political support.
propositions.quote: Ms. Dabar is a citizen of Djibouti. She alleges that because of her support for the Mouvement pour le renouveau démocratique et le développement [MRD], an opposition party, the police severely assaulted her and closed her store, taking away all her stock.

propositions.text: RPD dismissed her refugee claim for lack of credibility; RAD appeal was dismissed; re-opening application also dismissed.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Protection Division [RPD] of the Immigration and Refugee Board [IRB] dismissed her claim, because it found her not to be credible. Her appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division [RAD] of the IRB was never perfected and was dismissed. Her application to re-open the case was dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Ms. Dabar fled Djibouti after alleged assault; RPD dismissed claim for credibility; RAD appeal and re-opening dismissed.

propositions.text: Ms. Dabar applied for PRRA citing risks from political opinion, ethnicity, gender, and mental illness.
propositions.quote: Ms. Dabar then applied for a PRRA. She relied on risks related to her political opinion, ethnicity, gender and mental illness.

propositions.text: PRRA officer found new evidence did not overcome RPD credibility findings on political opinion.
propositions.quote: With respect to political opinion, the PRRA officer found that the new evidence filed by Ms. Dabar did not overcome the RPD’s credibility findings.

propositions.text: Officer acknowledged discrimination against women but noted Ms. Dabar operated business, is married, and has family support.
propositions.quote: The officer then acknowledged the documentary evidence regarding discrimination against women in Djibouti, in particular against single women, but noted that Ms. Dabar successfully operated a business, that she is still married and that she could rely on her family’s support.

propositions.text: Officer found little evidence Ms. Dabar would be personally affected by ethnic discrimination.
propositions.quote: The officer also found that there was little evidence that Ms. Dabar would be personally affected by discrimination based on her ethnic origin.

propositions.text: Officer found origin of Ms. Dabar’s PTSD unclear and that remote treatment might be possible if local support limited.
propositions.quote: Lastly, with respect to mental illness, the officer found that the origin of Ms. Dabar’s post-traumatic stress disorder [PTSD] was unclear, and that she could pursue remote treatment over the Internet if mental health support in Djibouti was too limited.

paragraphs.summary: Court reports PRRA officer found new evidence insufficient on political opinion, acknowledged gender discrimination but noted Ms. Dabar's business and family support, found little ethnic risk, and unclear PTSD origin.

propositions.text: Dismissing application because PRRA officer’s decision was reasonable with logical analysis despite some wording issues.
propositions.quote: I am dismissing Ms. Dabar’s application, because the PRRA officer’s decision was reasonable. The officer did not misapprehend the evidence and provided a logical chain of analysis to justify the rejection of Ms. Dabar’s claim. Certain aspects of the reasons could have been more carefully worded, but this do not affect the reasonableness of the whole.

propositions.text: Judicial review is not a line-by-line error search and only intervenes if officer fundamentally misapprehended evidence.
propositions.quote: After all, judicial review is not a “line-by-line treasure hunt for error”: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paragraph 102, [2019] 4 SCR 653 [Vavilov]. Neither is judicial review an opportunity to advocate for a different weighing of the evidence. The Court will intervene only if the officer “fundamentally misapprehended or failed to account for the evidence before it”: Vavilov, at paragraph 126.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses application as PRRA officer’s decision was reasonable; judicial review only intervenes for fundamental misapprehension of evidence.

propositions.text: Relied mainly on psychotherapist’s report alleging persecution based on mental health condition.
propositions.quote: In her PRRA application, Ms. Dabar relied mainly on the report of a psychotherapist to allege that her return to Djibouti would expose her to persecution based on her mental health condition.

propositions.text: Psychotherapist’s report recounts political persecution allegations found not credible and mentions ethnic discrimination not challenged.
propositions.quote: The report recounts her allegations of persecution based on political opinion, which were found not credible by the RPD. It also mentions discrimination based on ethnicity; the PRRA officer found that this did not amount to a personalized risk of persecution and Ms. Dabar does not challenge that aspect of the decision.

propositions.text: Report states Ms. Dabar has PTSD symptoms and treatment sessions, warns lack of trauma-informed services may worsen symptoms.
propositions.quote: The report then states that Ms. Dabar exhibits certain symptoms consistent with PTSD, briefly describes the treatment sessions she is undergoing and concludes by stating that “[t]he lack of support and appropriate trauma informed services may exasperate [sic] Mrs. Abdi Dabar’s symptoms mentioned above and impede her recovery.”

propositions.text: Relies on country evidence showing mental health services largely non-existent in Djibouti.
propositions.quote: Ms. Dabar also relies on country condition evidence showing that mental health services are largely non-existent in Djibouti.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant relies on psychotherapist’s report and country evidence showing lack of mental health services in Djibouti.

propositions.text: Argued removal would exacerbate PTSD due to abuse origin and lack of treatment, plus discrimination against mental illness.
propositions.quote: Based on this evidence, Ms. Dabar argued that her removal to Djibouti would exacerbate her condition, because this is where the abuse that caused her PTSD occurred. She also alleged that the lack of treatment would be detrimental to her mental health, and that there is discrimination against persons with a mental health condition in Djibouti.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues removal to Djibouti would worsen PTSD, lack of treatment, and mental health discrimination.

propositions.text: PRRA officer reasonably rejected submissions due to unclear PTSD origin and lack of proof of abuses.
propositions.quote: In my view, the PRRA officer reasonably rejected these submissions. First, as the allegations of political persecution were found not credible, it is unclear what the source of Ms. Dabar’s symptoms is.

propositions.text: Reasonable to give little weight to psychotherapist’s fear assertion and conclude insufficient evidence of abuses.
propositions.quote: While the officer accepted the psychotherapist’s statement that Ms. Dabar has symptoms consistent with PTSD, the origin of these symptoms has not been proved. Thus, it was reasonable to give little weight to the psychotherapist’s assertion that Ms. Dabar is “fearful of having to return to Djibouti due to her previous association with the opposition and the possible consequences.” It was equally reasonable for the officer to conclude that “[a]s for returning to the place where she suffered abuses, as previously demonstrated, I find there is insufficient evidence to establish such abuses occurred.”

paragraphs.summary: Court finds PRRA officer reasonably rejected submissions due to unclear PTSD origin and insufficient evidence of abuses.

propositions.text: Argued officer cannot disregard psychotherapist’s factual basis without hearing and implied credibility finding.
propositions.quote: In this connection, Ms. Dabar argued that the PRRA officer could not disregard the “factual basis” of the psychotherapist’s report without making an implied credibility finding, which cannot be done unless a hearing is held.

propositions.text: Disagrees; assumes events did not occur due to no challenge to credibility findings; PRRA applicant cannot overcome negative credibility by repeating story to health professional.
propositions.quote: I disagree. As she does not challenge the PRRA officer’s findings regarding ethnicity and, most importantly, political persecution, I must assume that the events she alleged did not take place. A PRRA applicant cannot overcome a previous negative credibility finding simply by telling the story found not credible to a health professional and have the professional repeat it in their report: Boyce v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 922 at paragraphs 52–62; Tacoa Veljovic v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 1069 at paragraph 44.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues officer cannot disregard psychotherapist’s factual basis without hearing; court disagrees, upholding credibility findings.

propositions.text: Reasonable to conclude removal despite PTSD symptoms does not amount to persecution.
propositions.quote: Second, it was reasonable for the officer to conclude that removing Ms. Dabar to Djibouti in spite of her PTSD symptoms does not amount to persecution.

propositions.text: Challenges officer’s statement that treatment could continue via Internet from Djibouti as problematic.
propositions.quote: Ms. Dabar takes issue with the officer’s statement that she could continue her psychological treatment through the Internet from Djibouti.

propositions.text: Agrees statement is problematic due to uncertain Internet and financial resources but this does not affect reasonableness of outcome.
propositions.quote: I agree that this statement is problematic, as it is unclear whether Ms. Dabar will have a sufficiently stable Internet connexion and the financial resources to pay for the treatment once she no longer lives in Canada. Nevertheless, this does not affect the reasonableness of the outcome,

propositions.text: Unavailability of health services generally not valid ground for refugee status; section 97 excludes risks from inability to provide adequate health care.
propositions.quote: because the unavailability of health services in a particular country is generally not understood as a valid ground to claim refugee status. Ms. Dabar has not provided any authority supporting the contrary proposition. With respect to risks covered by section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [the Act], subparagraph 97(1)(b)(iv) explicitly excludes risks flowing from a country’s “inability” to provide adequate health care.

propositions.text: Covarrubias confirms health service unavailability is excluded from refugee risk under section 97.
propositions.quote: See, in this regard, Covarrubias v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FCA 365 at paragraphs 20–41, [2007] 3 FCR 169.

propositions.text: Issues about mental health services availability are better addressed under humanitarian and compassionate grounds, not PRRA.
propositions.quote: In this regard, one should not confuse a PRRA and an application for relief on humanitarian and compassionate grounds pursuant to section 25 of the Act. Issues regarding the availability of mental health services are more properly addressed under the latter process.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds removal despite PTSD symptoms not persecution; health service unavailability excluded from refugee risk; humanitarian grounds more appropriate.

propositions.text: Reasonably rejected argument of widespread mental health stigma due to lack of evidence of personal persecution risk.
propositions.quote: Third, the PRRA officer reasonably rejected Ms. Dabar’s argument that “there is widespread social stigma and discrimination surrounding mental health issues in Djibouti”, as she failed to point to any evidence supporting this assertion and showing that she would be personally affected to the point that it would amount to persecution.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds officer reasonably rejected mental health stigma argument for lack of evidence of personal persecution risk.

propositions.text: Challenges rejection of gender-based persecution allegations despite evidence of discrimination against women in Djibouti.
propositions.quote: Ms. Dabar also challenges the rejection of her allegations of persecution based on gender. She provided evidence that women in Djibouti are subject to various forms of discrimination.

propositions.text: Officer acknowledged discrimination but found Ms. Dabar operated business and no indication conditions worsened.
propositions.quote: The PRRA officer acknowledged that there is discrimination against women, but found that these conditions existed when Ms. Dabar was living in Djibouti and did not prevent her from operating a business. The officer also noted that there was no indication that these conditions had deteriorated since then.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant challenges rejection of gender persecution; officer acknowledged discrimination but found no worsening and Ms. Dabar operated business.

propositions.text: Argues officer’s reasoning was backward-looking instead of forward-looking risk assessment.
propositions.quote: Ms. Dabar argues that the officer’s reasoning amounts to a backward-looking assessment of risk instead of the forward-looking assessment mandated by sections 96 and 97 of the Act.

propositions.text: Disagrees; officer entitled to rely on past experience to assess future risk; no evidence of deterioration means unlikely future persecution.
propositions.quote: I disagree. The officer was entitled to rely on Ms. Dabar’s past experience to conclude that she would not face the kind of serious, systematic discrimination that rises to the level of persecution in the future. She has been able to operate a business for at least two years despite her gender. Thus, given that she did not point to evidence documenting a deterioration of gender discrimination in Djibouti since her departure, Ms. Dabar is unlikely to face gender-based persecution in the future, which is the threshold that she must meet under section 96 of the Act. This does not make the assessment backward-looking.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues officer’s reasoning was backward-looking; court disagrees, finding reliance on past experience proper for future risk assessment.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably found Ms. Dabar could rely on family for transitional assistance despite their poverty.
propositions.quote: It was also reasonable for the PRRA officer to find that Ms. Dabar could rely on her family for assistance when returning to Djibouti. In her statutory declaration in support of her PRRA application, Ms. Dabar stated that she has a sister and two brothers in Djibouti, but added that they are poor and that it would be difficult for her to live with them. Given this, it was not unreasonable for the PRRA officer to find that her family would at least be able to provide transitional assistance.

paragraphs.summary: Officer reasonably found Ms. Dabar could rely on family for transitional assistance despite their poverty.

propositions.text: Argues officer’s finding that she operated business was contrary to evidence of forced closure.
propositions.quote: In her written submissions, Ms. Dabar argues that the PRRA officer’s finding that she could operate a business in Djibouti was contrary to the evidence, because she was forced to close down her store.

propositions.text: Must assume events of forced closure did not occur due to RPD findings; officer’s finding not unreasonable.
propositions.quote: However, as I explained earlier, I must proceed on the basis that these events did not take place. While Ms. Dabar claimed that the government forcibly closed her store in October 2016, the RPD found that she operated her business until March 2017 and, as a result, that it was not shut down by the government. Given these findings, Ms. Dabar has not persuaded me that the PRRA officer’s finding is unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues forced closure of business; court assumes it did not occur per RPD and finds officer’s finding reasonable.

propositions.text: Challenges specific statements about short stay in Somaliland and current support in Canada as incorrect.
propositions.quote: Ms. Dabar also challenges specific statements in the PRRA decision concerning a short stay in Somaliland and the manner in which she presently supports herself in Canada.

propositions.text: These statements do not affect officer’s analysis of persecution grounds and are not determinative.
propositions.quote: While these statements may be incorrect, they do not appear to play any role in the officer’s analysis of Ms. Dabar’s four asserted grounds of persecution, in a subsequent part of their reasons. I am not persuaded that they play any determinative role in the PRRA officer’s reasoning.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant challenges some factual statements; court finds they do not affect officer’s analysis or reasoning.

propositions.text: PRRA officer’s decision was reasonable; judicial review application dismissed; no question certified.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, the PRRA officer’s decision was reasonable. Accordingly, Ms. Dabar’s application for judicial review will be dismissed. JUDGMENT in IMM-8522-21 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The application for judicial review is dismissed. No question is certified.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes PRRA officer’s decision reasonable and dismisses judicial review application with no question certified.
